Kxd1 takes the knight. White is still winning because the h-pawn is too distant for the black king; the extra b3 pawn remains on the board.

nodes.explanation: h4+ forces Kf5. Then g4+ forces the h-pawn onto g4, and Rf4+ forces the bishop onto f4. Those black pieces become barriers when e4 delivers mate.

nodes.explanation: Rd5 blocks Bf3’s diagonal to a8. The d-pawn is still stopped by the rook on its file, so White should promote the a-pawn.

nodes.question: The bishop captured on d5. Does the same pawn promote?
nodes.explanation: Bd5 blocks Rd2’s file toward d8. The bishop still sees a8, so this time White should promote the d-pawn.

exercises.prompt: Why does the rook on d5 help the a-pawn?
exercises.answer: It blocks its own bishop’s diagonal from f3 to a8. The same rook still stops d8, so choose a8=Q.

exercises.prompt: Why do the roles reverse when the bishop takes on d5?
exercises.answer: The bishop blocks its rook’s d-file, freeing d8. Its own diagonal to a8 remains open, so promoting a8 would let it capture.

nodes.question: How can the knight dislodge the back-rank rook?
nodes.explanation: After ...Kxg4, White has a knight and b7 pawn against a rook and two pawns. Nc6 attacks Rd8 while guarding b8.

nodes.question: Why not promote immediately while the knight guards b8?
nodes.explanation: A rook sacrifice on b8 would remove White’s last pawn. The stronger plan is to improve the king and knight first.

rLE0oYWeGWY.title: Double Trouble
